title: How to build a snow cave (or a snow-mound shelter when there is no deep drift)

answer: Before you dig, check the slope for avalanche danger. The Army cold-weather manual warns that lee slopes, where wind-driven snow is deposited, can increase exposure to avalanche hazards (if the slope is steep enough, the snow eventually slides), and says: in snow-covered mountains, or when snowfall is imminent, always examine a slope's potential for an avalanche before setting up a bivouac on it.

Keep off slopes that could slide, and out from under them. FEMA says to avoid slopes steeper than 30 degrees and areas downhill of steep slopes, and to watch for signs of increased danger, including recent avalanches and shooting cracks along slopes. The Army cold-weather manual says to avoid avalanche-prone slopes at all costs. The Army survival manual says leeward slopes collect snow blown from the windward sides, forming slabs or sluffs, and tells you to consider, when selecting a shelter site, whether it is in an area free from the threat of avalanches.

Find a snowdrift at least 10 feet (about 3 meters) deep. The Army cold-weather manual says a suitable site is normally on the lee side of a steep ridge or riverbank, where drifted snow collects and becomes wind packed. That is the same kind of slope the avalanche warnings above are about, so make the avalanche check first. Do not use newly fallen, powdery or loose snow. If no drift is deep enough, use the snow-mound shelter in the last steps.
Test the depth of the drift with a sharpened branch or young tree about 13 feet (about 4 meters) long, or with a ski or ski pole.
Choose the entrance carefully, so that wind does not blow into the cave or block the entrance with drifting snow. Build it about 45 degrees from the downwind side.
Diggers get wet from sweat and from the snow. Wear a minimum amount of clothing while digging, so that you have a change of dry clothes when finished.

Burrow a small tunnel directly into the side of the snowdrift for 3 feet (about 1 meter). Excavate a chamber from this tunnel to the right and to the left, so that the length of the chamber is at right angles to the tunnel entrance.

Make the cave high enough to sit in comfortably. Arch the roof, for strength and so that drops of water run down the roof and sides instead of falling on the floor. Make the roof about a foot (30 cm) thick; the Army survival manual says the walls and ceiling should be at least 30 centimeters (1 foot) thick.
Put the sleeping area on a higher level than the highest point of the tunnel entrance, where the air is warmer. The tunnel entrance leads to the lowest level, where equipment is stored.
Separate the sleeping platform from the walls, or dig a small trench between the platform and the wall, so that melting snow does not wet you and your equipment.

Use at least two ventilation holes, one in the roof and one in the door. Inspect them every 2 or 3 hours to make sure they are not clogged with snow or ice. A ski pole stuck through the roof hole clears it from the inside.
Insulate the ground with all available materials, such as ponchos, cardboard, brush and boughs.
To keep the cave warm, block the entrance with a rucksack, poncho or snow block when it is not in use.
Mark the entrance by placing a pair of skis or other equipment upright on each side of the entryway.

If there is no drift large enough for a snow cave: pile snow into a mound and dig into that instead (a molded-dome shelter, or quinzhee). Even light powder snow solidifies enough once it is disturbed and shoveled into a mound. The remaining steps are the Army cold-weather manual's guidelines, written for a shelter for two people.

Mound shelter: clear an area down to the ground, at least 2 feet (about 61 cm) wider and 2 feet longer than a pair of sleeping mats placed side by side. Place a ski pole upright in the center, and a second pole along the ground toward one of the long ends.

Mound shelter: pile snow back into the area. After piling up 2 to 3 feet (about 61 to 91.5 cm) of snow, walk on the area to pack the snow down. Keep piling, stopping from time to time to pack the snow down, into a dome at least 5 feet (about 1.5 meters) tall.
Mound shelter: let the snow set for about 3 to 4 hours, then check that it has hardened enough. If it has not, wait until it does (repacking the area if needed) before you tunnel in.

Mound shelter: when the snow has hardened, tunnel in from one of the long ends of the dome, along the pole on the ground, at or just above ground level, and remove snow until you reach the center pole. Then widen the sleeping area until two people can fit inside, digging the entire living area down to ground level, or as close to the ground as possible: the Army cold-weather manual says this shelter should not have a sleeping bench.

Mound shelter: make the ceiling arched and smooth to prevent dripping, and make the walls at least 8 to 10 inches (about 20 to 25.5 cm) thick. Ceilings melt with time, which increases the inside dimensions of the shelter.

Mound shelter: seal the entrance (Army cold-weather manual) and install a ventilation shaft (Army survival manual). The survival manual says all openings except ventilation holes should be sealed, and that besides the ventilation hole through the roof another vent may be required at the door for adequate circulation of air.
warnings: Avalanche danger: this library gives only a few warning signs, such as those in the first steps, and no method for judging a slope. FEMA says to take a training course to learn how to identify hazardous conditions and places to avoid; the Army cold-weather manual says very specialized training is required to even come close to negotiating avalanche-prone slopes safely.
Do not walk on the roof: it can collapse.

Carbon monoxide is a deadly, odorless gas. Candles, fuel gel and small oil lamps produce it: leave the vent holes open, and take extra care to keep the air in the shelter fresh when cooking or heating. Make sure stoves and lanterns are working properly, and shut the stove off when sleeping unless someone stays awake as a guard.

Signs of carbon monoxide poisoning: headache, dizziness, confusion, yawning, weariness, nausea and ringing in the ears; a bright red color on lips and skin; drowsiness and sudden collapse. Suspect it if someone is found unconscious in an enclosed shelter.

If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning: move the person to open air and keep them still and warm. If they are not breathing, give mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, and CPR if necessary. Evacuate them immediately to the nearest medical treatment facility, and give oxygen immediately if available.

Cooking and heating inside, sources differ: FEMA's home guidance says camp stoves should always be used outdoors. The Army manuals describe cooking or heating in a snow cave only with the vent holes open and extra care for fresh air; the Army survival manual says to use the lower entrance area for cooking.

The Army cold-weather manual's emergency guidance for people lost where there are no trees says: do not use the gasoline stove to heat the shelter. Use it only to prepare hot food and drinks, conserve the fuel supply, and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.
If you cannot see your breath, the snow shelter is too warm. Cool it down to prevent melting and dripping.
A snow cave takes time and energy to build, you will get wet while building it, and building it requires practice. The most critical decision is when and where to stop and build the shelter.

quotes.text: During high winds, lee slopes may offer shelter. However, they can also increase exposure to avalanche hazards if wind-driven snow is deposited on lee slopes. If the slope is steep enough, the snow eventually slides. In snowcovered mountains or when snowfall is imminent, always examine a slope’s potential for an avalanche prior to establishing a bivouac upon it.
Watch for signs of increased danger, including recent avalanches and shooting cracks along slopes. Avoid areas of increased risk like slopes steeper than 30 degrees or areas downhill of steep slopes.
Take a training course to learn how to identify hazardous conditions, places to avoid, and the right way to use safety and rescue equipment.
As far as avalanche prone slopes are concerned, avoid them at all costs. Very specialized training is required to even come close to negotiating them safely.
Leeward slopes collect snow that has been blown from the windward sides, forming slabs or sluffs, depending upon the temperature and moisture.
When selecting a shelter site, consider whether the site
Is located in an area free from threat of avalanches, rockslides, mudslides, Flash-flood areas and high-water marks.

A snow cave can be used as an improvised shelter in open areas where deep and compacted snow is available. Normally, a suitable site is located on the lee side of a steep ridge or riverbank where drifted snow collects and becomes wind packed. The tunnel entrance gives access to the lowest level of the chamber. This is the bottom of the pit where equipment is stored.

When building the snow cave, locate a snowdrift at least 10 feet (approximately 3 meters) deep. Newly fallen, powdery, or loose snow should not be used. The depth of a snowdrift can be tested with a sharpened branch or young tree about 13 feet (approximately 4 meters) long, or with a ski or shorter ski pole. The entrance is chosen carefully so that wind does not blow into the cave or block the entrance with drifting snow. The entrance should be built so that it is about 45 degrees from the downwind side. A small tunnel is burrowed directly into the side of the snowdrift for 3 feet (approximately 1 meter). A chamber is excavated from this tunnel. Excavation is done to the right and left, so that the length of the chamber is at right angles to the tunnel entrance.
Personnel doing the digging become wet from perspiration and the snow inside the cave. They should wear a minimum amount of clothing to ensure they have a change of dry clothes when finished.

Make the snow cave high enough to provide a comfortable sitting space. The sleeping area is on a higher level than the highest point of the tunnel entrance, where there is warmer air. The roof is arched for strength and so that drops of water forming on the inside do not fall on the floor. This water follows along the curvature of the roof and sides, causing the walls to glaze over when frozen. The roof is about a foot (30 cm) thick.

Build the sleeping platform higher than the entrance. Separate the sleeping platform from the snow cave’s walls or dig a small trench between the platform and the wall. This platform will prevent the melting snow from wetting you and your equipment.
Block the entrance with a snow block or other material and use the lower entrance area for cooking. The walls and ceiling should be at least 30 centimeters (1 foot) thick.

To ensure that the cave is warm, the entrance should be blocked with a rucksack, poncho, or snow block when not in use. All available materials such as ponchos, cardboard from ration boxes, brush, and boughs should be used for ground insulation. Walking on the roof can cause it to collapse. At least two ventilator holes are used, one in the roof and one in the door. A ski pole can be stuck through the roof ventilator to clear it from the inside. The ventilation holes are inspected every 2 or 3 hours to ensure they have not become clogged with snow or ice. Extra care is taken to keep the air in the cave fresh when cooking or heating. The entrance should be marked by placing a pair of skis, or other equipment, upright on each side of the entryway.
Install a ventilation shaft. If you do not have a drift large enough to build a snow cave, you can make a variation of it by piling snow into a mound large enough to dig out.

In alpine regions and other barren locations, shelter can be constructed by piling up a large mound of snow and then digging into it. Even light powder snow solidifies enough once it is disturbed and shoveled into a mound. This is similar in appearance to a snow cave and referred to as a molded-dome shelter or quinzhee shelter.

Although the quinzhee shelter may look like a snow cave, this molded dome should not have a sleeping bench. Soldiers dig the entire living area down to ground level (or as close to the ground as possible) and seal the entrance as they would for a thermal shelter. For best results, follow these guidelines:

When constructing a quinzhee shelter for two Soldiers, clear an area down to the ground: The area should be at least 2 feet (approximately 61 cm) wider and 2 feet longer than a pair of sleeping mats placed side by side. Place a ski pole upright, in the center. Place a second pole along the ground towards one of the long ends.

Begin to pile snow back into the area. After piling up 2 to 3 feet (approximately 61 to 91.5 cm) of snow, walk on the area to pack the snow down. Continue to pile snow, periodically stopping to pack the snow down into a dome at least 5 feet (approximately 1.5 meters) tall.
Let the snow set for about 3 to 4 hours: After this time, check that the snow has sufficiently hardened. If it has not, wait until it does, possibly repacking the area.

If the snow has hardened, begin to tunnel in from one of the long ends of the dome along the ski pole, at or just above ground level. Remove snow until reaching the center pole. Begin to widen the sleeping area until two Soldiers can fit inside. The ceiling should be arched and smooth to prevent dripping. Ceilings melt with time, increasing the internal dimensions of the shelter. Make the walls at least 8 to 10 inches (approximately 20 to 25.5 cm) thick.

All openings except ventilation holes should be sealed to avoid heat loss. Leaving vent holes open is especially important if heat-producing devices are used (see figure 6-14, page 6-16). Candles, fuel gel, or small oil lamps produce carbon monoxide. In addition to the ventilation hole through the roof, another vent may be required at the door to ensure adequate circulation of air. As a rule, if isolated persons cannot see their breath, the snow shelter is too warm and should be cooled down to preclude melting and dripping.
Remember that it takes time and energy to build and that you will get wet while building it.
Building a snow cave requires practice. Large shelters are usually more efficient for squad-size and larger units. The most critical decision is when and where to stop and build the shelter.

Whenever a squad stove fire, fuel-fired heater, or internal combustion engine is used indoors, there is danger of carbon monoxide poisoning. Fresh air in living and working quarters is vital. Carbon monoxide is a deadly, odorless gas that displaces oxygen in the blood stream. To prevent carbon monoxide poisoning— Ensure that stoves and lanterns are functioning properly. Do not let Soldiers warm themselves by engine exhaust. Always crack the windows in vehicles when a heater is in use, and do not allow anyone to sleep in a running vehicle. Use a tent guard or shut the stove off when sleeping.

If a Soldier is found unconscious in an enclosed shelter, carbon monoxide poisoning be suspected. Common symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning are— Headache, dizziness, confusion, yawning, weariness, nausea, and ringing in the ears. Bright red color on lips and skin. Drowsiness and sudden collapse.

Adhere to the following for proper treatment of carbon monoxide poisoning: Move the Soldier to open air. Keep the victim still and warm. If the Soldier is not breathing, administer mouth-to-mouth resuscitation. Administer cardiopulmonary resuscitation, if necessary. Immediately evacuate the Soldier to the nearest medical treatment facility. Immediately administer oxygen, if available.
Avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. Generators, camp stoves, or charcoal grills should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows. Never use a gas stovetop or oven to heat your home.

If lost in an area where there are no trees, do not use the gasoline stove to heat the shelter. The stove is used only to prepare hot food and drinks. Conserve the fuel supply and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.

conflict: (1) Site and avalanche: TC 21-3 (2025) para 7-17 says a suitable snow-cave site is normally 'on the lee side of a steep ridge or riverbank where drifted snow collects and becomes wind packed'; its para 5-12 says lee slopes 'can also increase exposure to avalanche hazards if wind-driven snow is deposited on lee slopes', its para 6-47 says of avalanche prone slopes 'avoid them at all costs', ATP 3-50.21 (2018) para 7-5 says 'Leeward slopes collect snow that has been blown from the windward sides, forming slabs or sluffs' and para 6-9 wants a shelter site 'free from threat of avalanches', and FEMA P-2064 (2020) says 'Avoid areas of increased risk like slopes steeper than 30 degrees or areas downhill of steep slopes'. The revised card puts the avalanche check first (steps 1 and 2), attributed, and step 3 says the 'steep ridge' site is the same kind of slope; TC 21-3's 'steep ridge' and FEMA's 30 degrees remain in tension and the owner may want to choose. No kit document says how to judge a slope beyond FEMA's signs (recent avalanches, shooting cracks); TC 21-3 para 6-47 says the warning signs 'are taught in the stationery avalanche awareness class', and the card's first warning now states this gap. (2) Stoves in an enclosed shelter: FEMA P-2064 (2020, power outage section, written for homes) says 'Generators, camp stoves, or charcoal grills should always be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows.' The Army manuals describe cooking or heating inside a snow cave with ventilation (TC 21-3 2025: 'Extra care is taken to keep the air in the cave fresh when cooking or heating'; ATP 3-50.21 2018: 'use the lower entrance area for cooking', 'Leaving vent holes open is especially important if heat-producing devices are used'). TC 21-3 itself also says, in its emergency guidance for people lost where there are no trees, 'do not use the gasoline stove to heat the shelter. The stove is used only to prepare hot food and drinks.' The card shows all of these; the owner must choose. (3) Snow-mound shelter (quinzhee), steps added in revision from TC 21-3 paras 7-22 and 7-23: ATP 3-50.21 para 6-27 only calls the mound 'a variation' of the snow cave (whose design has a sleeping platform higher than the entrance) and lists 'Install a ventilation shaft' just before it; TC 21-3 says the quinzhee 'should not have a sleeping bench' and that the living area is dug 'down to ground level'. The card follows TC 21-3's detailed quinzhee guidelines and says so. TC 21-3 says to 'seal the entrance as they would for a thermal shelter', a term the kit does not explain, and gives no ventilation guidance for the quinzhee; the card adds ATP 3-50.21 para 6-39 ('All openings except ventilation holes should be sealed', 'another vent may be required at the door'), attributed. TC 21-3's quinzhee sizes are written 'for two Soldiers'; the card says two people.

review.notes: Pass. (1) Previous findings fixed: the avalanche check is now steps 1-2, attributed (TC 21-3 5-12: examine a slope's avalanche potential before a bivouac; FEMA P-2064 avalanche section: avoid slopes steeper than 30 degrees and areas downhill of steep slopes, watch for recent avalanches and shooting cracks; TC 21-3 6-47: avoid at all costs; ATP 3-50.21 7-5 leeward slabs and 6-9 site free from avalanche threat), step 3 ties TC 21-3's 'lee side of a steep ridge' site to those warnings, and warning 1 says plainly that the kit has no method for judging a slope. The snow-mound (quinzhee) steps are added from TC 21-3 7-22/7-23 and verified: clear an area 2 ft wider and longer than two mats, poles, pack after 2-3 ft, dome at least 5 ft, let it set 3-4 h and check it has hardened before tunnelling, tunnel along the ground pole, dig to ground level with no sleeping bench, arched smooth ceiling, walls at least 8-10 in; seal plus vent from ATP 6-27/6-39, attributed. Cooking conflict kept attributed, with ATP's 'use the lower entrance area for cooking'. Warnings cut from 11 to 9 (radio and buddy lines gone). (2) Every line re-checked against its quote: drift 10 ft, 13-ft probe, entrance 45 degrees from downwind, 3-ft tunnel, chamber at right angles, minimal clothing while digging, sitting height, arched roof about 1 ft (TC) and at least 1 ft (ATP), sleeping area above the entrance, trench, two vents checked every 2-3 h, insulation, entrance block, marked entrance, CO prevention, signs and treatment (TC 21-3 4-48 ff.), the cannot-see-your-breath rule, practice and time. 'Shut the stove off when sleeping unless someone stays awake as a guard' is a fair plain rendering of TC 21-3's 'Use a tent guard or shut the stove off when sleeping'. FEMA's camp-stove line is correctly labelled home guidance (it sits in P-2064's power-outage bullets). (3) Conflicts (lee-side site vs avalanche, stoves inside, quinzhee bench and vent) are shown attributed in the card text. (4) Nothing safety-critical in TC 21-3 7-17..7-23 or ATP 3-50.21 6-25..6-27 and 6-39 is left out. (5) All asks answered (roof thickness, vents, depth, no-drift mound, blizzard). (6) Protocol; lines are real steps, and step 3 sends readers without a deep drift to the mound steps. Optional: the CO treatment line could point to the CPR card once that card passes. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Fail. (1) Drafter flag, lee side vs avalanche - verdict: not two sources disagreeing but one hazard split across the card. Step 1 sends the reader to 'the lee side of a steep ridge' where drifts become wind packed (TC 21-3 7-17), and the avalanche check appears only as warning 1. TC 21-3 5-12 and ATP 3-50.21 7-5 ('Leeward slopes collect snow that has been blown from the windward sides, forming slabs or sluffs'; 'Avoid possible avalanches') say that same terrain can slide. A lay person following the numbered steps can dig into a loaded slope. Fix: put the avalanche check into step 1 (or a step before it): before digging, examine the slope's potential for an avalanche; lee slopes collect wind-blown snow that can slide (TC 21-3, ATP 3-50.21); FEMA says avoid slopes steeper than 30 degrees and areas downhill of steep slopes. Keep it attributed, since TC 21-3's 'steep ridge' and FEMA's 30 degrees are in tension. (2) The last step (pile snow into a mound and dig it out, ATP 6-27) omits the kit's safety-critical details for that shelter: TC 21-3 7-22/7-23 (quinzhee) says pack the snow while piling, dome at least 5 feet, let the snow set about 3 to 4 hours and check it has hardened before tunnelling, walls at least 8 to 10 inches, no sleeping bench (dig the living area to ground level). Digging an unset mound risks collapse. Fix: add those lines attributed, or drop the step and make a separate quinzhee card. (3) Drafter flag, cooking inside - verdict: handled correctly and attributed (Army in-cave cooking/heating only with vents open and extra care for fresh air; FEMA's camp-stove line labelled as home guidance; TC 21-3's no-trees rule); keep. If cooking is mentioned, add ATP 6-27's 'use the lower entrance area for cooking'. Everything else verified: drift 10 ft, 13-ft probe, entrance 45 degrees from downwind, 3-ft tunnel, chamber at right angles, minimal clothing while digging, roof about 1 ft (TC) / at least 1 ft (ATP) both shown, sleeping area above the entrance, trench, two vents checked every 2-3 h, ground insulation, entrance block, marked entrance, CO prevention/signs/treatment (TC 21-3 4-48 ff.). Minor: 11 warnings dilute the critical ones (avalanche, CO); the generic radio and buddy-system lines could go.
